title: The Invasions from the North-West
subtitle: Ghaznavids, Ghurids and the transformation of northern India

hero.title: THE NORTH-WESTERN INVASIONS
hero.subtitle: From Frontier Raids to Permanent Rule
hero.summary: A chronological overview of the military and political expansion from the north-west into northern India, from frontier warfare to the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate.

abstract: This overview provides the framework for studying the medieval invasion period as a sequence of changing political and military systems rather than a single undifferentiated event.

sections.title: THE FIRST PHASE — FRONTIER CONQUEST
content: The north-western frontier had long been contested. Arab expansion into Sindh in the eighth century created an early Islamic political foothold, while later Turkic powers emerged from Afghanistan and Central Asia.
The Hindu Shahi kingdom became one of the principal powers confronting the Ghaznavids.

sections.title: THE GHAZNAVID SYSTEM
content: Mahmud of Ghazni transformed repeated Indian campaigning into a major component of Ghaznavid state power. Wealth, captives, political prestige and religious legitimacy reinforced one another.
The campaigns were devastating in particular places, but they were not equivalent to the permanent occupation of all northern India.

sections.title: THE GHURID TURN
content: The Ghurids altered the strategic pattern by seeking durable political control. Muhammad of Ghor's campaigns against the Rajput powers eventually produced the decisive battles of Tarain.
The victory of 1192 created the conditions for the expansion of Ghurid authority in Delhi and the later consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate.

sections.title: WHAT CHANGED FOR HINDU SOCIETY?
content: The consequences differed across regions. Some rulers became tributaries or allies; others were displaced. Temples could be destroyed, taxed, appropriated or protected depending on political circumstances. Captivity and enslavement accompanied some campaigns.
The historical experience was therefore uneven but profoundly important for political, social and religious history.

sections.title: THE LONGER CONSEQUENCE
content: The establishment of durable Muslim-ruled states in northern India created a new political order. Yet Hindu kingdoms, institutions and cultural traditions continued to exist and in many regions flourished.
The result was not the replacement of one civilisation by another, but a prolonged and often violent interaction between political traditions, religions and cultures.

sections.title: READING THE PERIOD WITHOUT FORGETTING BHARAT
content: A Hindu-centred history should not hide the violence of conquest. Nor should it turn every medieval Muslim into a caricature or every political event into a religious war.

The most useful approach is to name rulers, armies, institutions and events precisely; document the suffering; honour resistance; and study the internal weaknesses that made repeated invasions possible.

chronology.event: Arab conquest of Sindh under Muhammad ibn Qasim.
Ghaznavid expansion from Afghanistan into the Punjab and northern India.
Death of Muhammad of Ghor and consolidation of the Delhi Sultanate's early political order.
